name: generator
intent: Produce a sequence on demand: a routine that yields one element at a time and suspends between elements, so its caller can consume a lazy - possibly unbounded - source with memory and work proportional to what it actually takes.
problem: Code must expose a sequence whose elements are not yet available - they are computed, read, paged or produced by a stateful process - and the two obvious shapes are both wrong. Materialising the sequence into a collection costs memory and latency, breaks on infinite or live sources and wastes every element the consumer never asks for; exposing the production loop to each caller (or pushing items through callbacks) instead leaks the producer's state, termination logic and error handling into every consumer, where they are duplicated and drift apart.
context: Applies wherever a sequence is produced rather than read from an existing container: streaming I/O, paginated APIs, pipeline stages over large data, on-demand or infinite series, and one-pass parsing or traversal whose next element depends on what the consumer does. It fits best when the consumer may stop early, when the number of elements is unknown or unbounded, or when holding the whole sequence is impossible; the toolchain decides only which realization is available (yield syntax, an iterator protocol, a callback iterator, a channel producer, or a hand-written state machine).
benefits: Work and memory are proportional to what is consumed: no intermediate collection is built, so large or unbounded sequences flow through constant memory and a consumer that stops early stops the production with it.
The producer reads as ordinary sequential code: per-element state lives in the routine's own frame across suspensions instead of in a hand-written cursor, index bookkeeping or a callback chain.

Production and consumption are decoupled: one producer plugs into any consumer or lazy adapter (for/for-in/for-await, map/filter/take/zip), so new sources are new routines rather than new classes and call sites.
Latency to the first element does not wait for the whole sequence: streaming responses, search with early exit and paginated reads hand back their first results immediately.

Side effects the consumer never demands never run: I/O, expensive computation and allocation happen at the moment an element is pulled, which makes partial consumption genuinely cheaper rather than merely lazier.
tradeoffs: Single-use resumable state: a generator object cannot be rewound, forked or inspected, so replayability, snapshots and concurrent traversal each need a different construct (a factory, a collection, or a fresh producer per consumer).

Timing becomes implicit: nothing runs until the first pull, so errors surface at the consumer far from the producing code and calling the producer no longer means the work has happened; parameter validation has to be hoisted into a wrapper deliberately.

Abandonment is a real failure mode: an unclosed generator keeps its frame - and any file, lock, connection or pool slot it opened - alive, and channel- or task-based producers can outlive the consumer that stopped early.

Per-element overhead: suspension and resumption, a compiler-generated state machine or a channel hand-off cost more than an index loop over an array, so hot numeric loops are the wrong place for a generator.

Debugging gets harder: stack traces are cut off at the suspension point, profilers attribute the time to the consumer, and the language-specific error channels (throw into the generator, GeneratorExit, Dispose, cancellation) must be understood to reason about failures.

Laziness does not survive every algorithm: sort, reverse, group-by, retry or any multi-pass logic forces materialisation, so a potentially unbounded producer has to be bounded - take(n), islice, limit or an explicit fuel parameter - before those consumers.

participants.responsibility: The code that knows how to produce the next element: it runs until a suspension point (yield/co_yield/yield callback), keeps per-element state in its own locals, and signals completion when the sequence ends.
The stateful handle returned to the caller: it stores the suspension point and locals, owns the underlying resource, and executes cleanup when it is closed, exhausted or collected.
Asks for one element at a time (next()/for/for-await), decides when to stop, and therefore controls how much work the producer performs.
Lazy transformations attached between producer and consumer (map/filter/take/chunk/zip) that keep per-element demand instead of buffering.
Materialises or reduces the sequence (collect/forEach/reduce/toList) and is the point where laziness ends and any forced buffering happens.

use_cases: Streaming and I/O: hand a caller one line, record or chunk at a time (file and socket readers, log tailing, CSV/JSON streaming) so nothing is fully resident and the read stops when the consumer stops.
Pagination and cursor walking: yield the items of page N, fetch page N+1 on the next pull, and let the consumer stop on the first match instead of walking every page.
Lazy pipelines over large data: map/filter/chunk transformations that must not materialise intermediate collections, including fused producer-consumer loops in ETL, reporting and log processing.
Unbounded or generated series: counters, IDs, timestamps, simulation steps, sensor and tick streams, and property-test inputs where the consumer decides how many elements to take.

Custom container traversal or views: expose a filtered or projected view of a data structure without building an intermediate list and without leaking its layout (tree walks, graph frontiers, sparse matrices).
Front of a producer-consumer pipeline: a routine that turns a source into a stream of work items (line-by-line parsing, chunked uploads, task enumeration) feeding workers, queues or async iterators.

Async streaming APIs: async def + yield for paginated REST/GraphQL, database cursors (EF Core AsAsyncEnumerable, JDBC streaming), WebSocket message streams, and SSE event sources where the consumer controls the pace via backpressure.
Event stream processing: consuming live event feeds (audit logs, IoT sensors, market data) where unbounded production meets selective consumption, and early exit saves both producer and network work.

Generator pipelines for data processing: composing async generators with filter/map/flatMap/reduce (or yield*) to build readable streaming ETL pipelines that stay lazy end-to-end without materialising intermediate collections.

Lazy file and network readers: line-by-line or chunk-wise reading of large files, HTTP streaming responses, or multipart downloads where memory must stay proportional to the chunk size regardless of total stream length.

Simulation and game loops: yielding game ticks, physics steps, or time-series values on demand so the simulation advances only as fast as the renderer consumes frames, keeping the model and view decoupled.
Property-based testing and fuzzing: generating arbitrary sequences on demand (while(true) yield random.choice(inputs)) so the test runner draws only as many values as it exercises.
Database cursor-style iteration: wrapping a paginated query behind a generator so callers can iterate without knowing whether the backend fetches rows one at a time or page by page.

Multi-source merging: using yield* or itertools.chain from multiple generators to interleave or concatenate streams (database + cache + network) while presenting a single uniform sequence to the caller.

Python asyncio async generators: expose paginated or socket data through async def + yield, consume with async for, and close early with aclose()/aclosing() so the event loop does not retain resources.
Browser Fetch streams: consume Response.body as a WHATWG ReadableStream with for await...of, processing chunks incrementally and using AbortController or stream cancellation when the caller stops.
.NET async streams: return IAsyncEnumerable<T> from paginated, GraphQL, or SignalR operations, consume with await foreach, and propagate cancellation with WithCancellation/[EnumeratorCancellation].
avoid_when: The consumer always needs every element and the sequence is finite: a plain loop or one materialised result is simpler, faster and easier to reason about than a generator.
Order, replay or random access matters: callers that index, re-iterate or pass the sequence around want a concrete collection or an array, not a single-pass source.
The elements are cheap and already in memory: iterating the existing collection directly avoids the single-use trap with no memory saving to compensate.
The consumer runs in another process, service or request: page or stream over that boundary with explicit leases and backpressure instead of shipping a live generator object.
Production is trivial and bounded (two or three elements, no state): returning a tuple, list or array is clearer and avoids the lifecycle rules entirely.
anti_patterns: Using a generator as a lazy substitute for validation or authorisation: elements reach the consumer before - or entirely without - the checks an eager load would have performed, and stopping early skips whatever cleanup the validation pass owned.

Caching the generator object and iterating it twice (a stored IEnumerable over one enumerator, a reused Iterator, a second for...of over the same JS generator): the second pass silently yields nothing.
Hiding an unbounded producer behind an eager sink: list(gen), ToList(), spread or collect over an infinite generator is an out-of-memory hang written as one line.

Hand-rolling a state-machine cursor in a language that has native generators (or adopting a coroutine library where a plain loop would do): paying either bookkeeping bugs or dependency and context-switch costs for no benefit.
Creating a generator per element inside a hot loop, so allocation and suspension overhead dominate the work being done.
Starting a generator for its side effects and never draining or closing it, leaving files, locks, background tasks or goroutines alive for the lifetime of the process.

Putting business-critical output into a generator's return value and consuming it with for await...of: the loop protocol silently discards the final return value. Yield the completion signal explicitly if the consumer needs it.
Creating a generator per element inside a hot loop: allocation and suspension overhead dominates the work being done. Prefer iterating directly or pooling generator instances.
Starting a generator for its side effects and never draining or closing it: files, locks, background tasks, goroutines, and database connections stay alive for the process lifetime.

For async generators in Python: using asend() without calling aclose() afterwards leaks the generator frame. The event loop only finalises generators on loop shutdown — not on early exit from async for.
Using blocking I/O inside an async generator (e.g., Python requests.get() instead of aiohttp): blocks the event loop thread, preventing other async tasks from making progress.

Not handling CancellationToken in async iterators: if the client disconnects mid-stream, the generator keeps running. Always accept and check the token, or wire it via [EnumeratorCancellation] (C#) / WithCancellation (Python) so disconnection propagates to the producer.

Calling MoveNextAsync() on a C# IAsyncEnumerator from multiple threads concurrently: the contract requires sequential calls. Parallel enumeration requires separate enumerator instances from GetAsyncEnumerator().

Type narrowing issues with generators in statically typed languages: the generator's return type may widen to yield type plus StopIteration, and consumers that do not handle all branches silently drop type information.
Ignoring the async vs sync boundary: passing a sync generator to code expecting async iteration (or vice versa) produces a TypeError or silent non-advancement that is hard to diagnose.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: generation and consumption are separate routines with an explicit boundary (the element stream) between them.
Information hiding: the consumer sees a sequence and a protocol, never the producer's state, buffers or indices - the suspended frame keeps them private.
Lazy evaluation as economic design: work happens only when an element is demanded, so cost tracks the benefit actually taken rather than the maximum possible output.
Single responsibility: the producer owns the state transitions between elements; the consumer owns the loop, the exit policy and the accumulation.
Uniformity and open/closed: one iteration protocol lets finite collections, unbounded series and stateful processes plug into the same consumers and adapters without special cases.
best_practices: Bound every producer that can be long or infinite at the call site: take(n)/islice/limit/takeWhile, or an explicit stop condition or fuel parameter inside the producer itself. An unbounded producer plus a materialising consumer is an infinite loop.

Make cleanup deterministic: close the generator on every exit path (try/finally plus close(), using/Dispose, defer plus cancel a context, contextlib.aclosing/async with aclosing). Never rely on garbage collection or process exit for cleanup — especially for async generators, which the event loop cannot reliably finalise without explicit aclose().

Prefer the language's native generator primitive and its iteration protocol so for/for-in/for-await and the adapter library work; hand-write a cursor only when the state must be inspected, serialised or split.
Keep per-pull work small and non-blocking: batch or buffer reads that would otherwise pay a suspension (or channel round-trip) per element, and leave heavy I/O to bulk operations behind the sequence.

Test laziness explicitly: pull a bounded prefix and assert with side-effect counters that later elements were never produced, instead of materialising the whole sequence in the test. Use tracemalloc in Python or allocation profilers to detect unclosed generator frames.

State single-use semantics in the API: say whether a call returns a fresh generator or a shared cursor, and prefer returning a fresh one (a generator factory or an iterable) over handing out a spent object.

For async generators, always wrap with aclosing() or async with aclosing() and propagate CancellationToken via [EnumeratorCancellation] (C#) or explicit token parameters. For JavaScript, prefer using/await using blocks or explicit gen.return() in finally to ensure cleanup fires on early break.

Avoid yielding from within try/except blocks that swallow exceptions — exceptions from the producer can hide in the generator frame and surface as StopIteration at unexpected consumer locations. Ensure all exceptions propagate cleanly.

For async generator pipelines (map/filter/compose), avoid pre-fetching or buffering ahead of the consumer; let the consumer drive the pace to preserve backpressure. When parallel processing is needed, use bounded queues rather than asyncio.gather on yielded values.

Prefer a final yield over a return value when the completion signal is meaningful to the consumer: for await...of silently ignores the generator's return value. Yield the final signal explicitly so early-exit consumers can observe it.
Keep the producer state inside the suspended frame, never in globals or shared fields, to prevent interference when the same generator factory is called concurrently by multiple consumers.
When combining generators (yield*), ensure the inner generator's cleanup propagates correctly through the delegation chain, especially with async generators and finally blocks.
